title: Verification, records and release boundaries
audience: Supervisors, coordinators and trained cleaners who may be asked to triage, refer or document mould-related work in homes, rentals and commercial buildings, under an approved plan. Not a qualification or authority to remediate, demolish, or certify any building or room.
learningOutcomes: Write a closeout report that separates task completion, visual review and independent clearance.
Refuse a clearance or pathogen-free statement from the crew.
Name the unverified areas and the reviewer with authority.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers records and the limits of what can be claimed. It does not give a clearance, a pathogen-free result or a reoccupation decision. A closeout report is not a certificate.

instruction.heading: Three things kept apart
instruction.body: Keep task completion, visual review and independent clearance apart. Task completion means the agreed work was done. Visual review means someone looked and recorded what could be seen. Independent clearance is a judgement made by a different, competent reviewer under the requirements that apply to the job. A visual clean cannot establish a pathogen-free result, so a cleaner who writes one has claimed something the work does not support. The WA guideline recommends that the post-remediation evaluation be done by a different entity from the one that carried out the work. It states that there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment or for who carries it out.

instruction.heading: The closeout report
instruction.body: Prepare a factual closeout report. Record the observations, the methods used as the plan sets them, the changes made, the limitations, the areas not verified, and who has authority for post-remediation verification. Do not describe unverified areas as safe. Reoccupation is a separate decision that follows the applicable local and contractual requirements, so the report does not declare a home safe to occupy.

procedure: Separate the record into three parts: task completion, visual review and independent clearance.
Record what was done and the methods used, as the plan sets them.
Record the observations, the changes made and the limitations.
List the areas not verified, and name who has authority for post-remediation verification.
Refuse any request from the crew for a pathogen-free or clearance statement.
Issue the closeout report, and keep a copy in the job file.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks for a pathogen-free certificate after the cleaner has finished a visual clean.
workedExamples.reasoning: Only what was done and what was seen. A visual clean cannot establish a pathogen-free result. Record the unverified areas, state that independent clearance is required, and name the reviewer who must give it.

workedExamples.situation: The crew finished the agreed work, and the manager wants the report to say the home is safe to reoccupy.
workedExamples.reasoning: It states the task completed, what was seen and the areas not verified. The reoccupation decision is separate and follows the applicable requirements, so the report does not declare the home safe.

equipmentAndPpe: Closeout report template with the three parts separated.
Job file for the copy of the report and the referral records.
Training-only fictional job file. No real certificate is issued in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Giving a pathogen-free or clearance certificate after a visual clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Separate task completion, visual review and independent clearance. Name the reviewer.
List unverified areas and state that they are not verified.

commonErrors.error: Treating task completion as reoccupation approval.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep reoccupation separate, and follow the applicable requirements.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A closeout report is not a clearance, a certificate or a reoccupation approval. Completing this lesson does not give a licence or authority to issue any of these.
The WA guideline states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment, or for who carries it out. Other jurisdictions were not checked for this lesson.

qualityStandard: The learner writes a closeout report that separates task completion, visual review and clearance.
The learner refuses a clearance or pathogen-free statement.
The learner names the unverified areas and the reviewer with authority.
documentationEvidence: Closeout report with observations, methods, changes, limitations and unverified areas.
Record of each refused clearance request, with the reason.
Named reviewer and the authority for post-remediation verification.
summary: A visual clean cannot prove a pathogen-free result.

knowledgeChecks.question: After a visual clean, a customer asks for a pathogen-free certificate. What can the cleaner write?
options: Only what was done and what was seen, with the unverified areas and the reviewer who must clear them.
A pathogen-free certificate, because the room looks clean.
That the room is safe for children.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is an independent clearance?
options: A judgement by a different, competent reviewer under the applicable requirements.
The customer's opinion that the room is clean.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the WA guideline say about legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment?
options: It requires a licensed assessor every time.
It requires a certificate signed by the resident.
It states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment or for who carries it out.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify that a building, room or occupant area is safe or free of mould or pathogens. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Restricted or high-exposure remediation is carried out only by an appropriately qualified and competent professional under an approved plan, and some related work, including asbestos and lead disturbance and certain waste handling, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. The owner, manager, tenant or contract may define what work is permitted, but where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. Where the controlling authority or the competent supervisor is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the hazards are unknown or changing; the work is destructive or hazardous and outside the authorised scope; exposure is uncontrolled or the building is unsafe to occupy; supervision, equipment or permissions are insufficient; flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present; a worker's PPE or respirator readiness has not been verified; a client asks for a clearance or pathogen-free statement; or a waste route is unauthorised. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it and restart only after the competent supervisor has confirmed the scope in writing.
